claim: De novo limb regeneration after amputation is restricted in mammals to the distal digit tip.
source: De novo limb regeneration after amputation is restricted in mammals to the distal digit tip.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about mammalian regenerative capacity.

claim: The blastema is a heterogeneous population of lineage-restricted, dedifferentiated cells that orchestrates regeneration of the amputated bone and surrounding soft tissue.
source: Central to this regenerative process is the blastema, a heterogeneous population of lineage-restricted, dedifferentiated cells that ultimately orchestrates regeneration of the amputated bone and surrounding soft tissue.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific understanding of blastema composition and function.

claim: Spatial transcriptomics was used to characterize the transcriptional profile specifically within the blastema.
source: To investigate skeletal regeneration, we made use of spatial transcriptomics to characterize the transcriptional profile specifically within the blastema.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: A gene signature with high specificity for the blastema was generated in both spatial data and previously published single-cell RNA-sequencing transcriptomic studies.
source: Using this technique, we generated a gene signature with high specificity for the blastema in both our spatial data, as well as other previously published single-cell RNA-sequencing transcriptomic studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Digit amputation in aged mice shows a significant impairment in regeneration compared to young mice.
source: Consistent with other forms of repair, our digit amputation mouse model showed a significant impairment in regeneration in aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing young and aged mice.

claim: Spatial analysis revealed a metabolic shift in aged blastema associated with an increased bioenergetic requirement.
source: Contrasting young and aged mice, spatial analysis revealed a metabolic shift in aged blastema associated with an increased bioenergetic requirement.
evidence: This is based on spatial transcriptomics data comparing young and aged mice.

claim: Enhanced metabolic turnover in aged mice was associated with increased hypoxia and angiogenic signaling.
source: This enhanced metabolic turnover was associated with increased hypoxia and angiogenic signaling, leading to excessive vascularization and altered regenerated bone architecture in aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in the study.

claim: Excessive vascularization and altered regenerated bone architecture occur in aged mice.
source: This enhanced metabolic turnover was associated with increased hypoxia and angiogenic signaling, leading to excessive vascularization and altered regenerated bone architecture in aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological and micro-CT data.

claim: Administration of oxaloacetate decreased the oxygen consumption rate of the aged blastema.
source: Administration of the metabolite oxaloacetate decreased the oxygen consumption rate of the aged blastema and increased WNT signaling, leading to enhanced in vivo bone regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse analysis data.

claim: Administration of oxaloacetate increased WNT signaling in aged blastema.
source: Administration of the metabolite oxaloacetate decreased the oxygen consumption rate of the aged blastema and increased WNT signaling, leading to enhanced in vivo bone regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by spatial transcriptomics data.

claim: Administration of oxaloacetate led to enhanced in vivo bone regeneration in aged mice.
source: Administration of the metabolite oxaloacetate decreased the oxygen consumption rate of the aged blastema and increased WNT signaling, leading to enhanced in vivo bone regeneration.
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT analysis of bone regeneration.

claim: Targeting cell metabolism may be a promising strategy to mitigate aging-induced declines in tissue regeneration.
source: Thus, targeting cell metabolism may be a promising strategy to mitigate aging-induced declines in tissue regeneration.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Amputation of the distal one-third of the terminal phalangeal element (P3) can regenerate.
source: This regenerative response is specific to the level of amputation: amputation of the distal one-third of the terminal phalangeal element (P3) can regenerate, whereas an amputation through the middle phalangeal element (P2) forms a hypertrophic callus of the bone.
evidence: This is established knowledge about digit regeneration.

claim: Amputation through the middle phalangeal element (P2) forms a hypertrophic callus of the bone.
source: This regenerative response is specific to the level of amputation: amputation of the distal one-third of the terminal phalangeal element (P3) can regenerate, whereas an amputation through the middle phalangeal element (P2) forms a hypertrophic callus of the bone.
evidence: This is established knowledge about digit regeneration.

claim: The regenerative response has been well documented in rodents, monkeys, and humans.
source: This regenerative response has been well documented in rodents, monkeys, and humans (Bryant et al., 2002; Brockes and Kumar, 2005; Han et al., 2008; Fernando et al., 2011; Simkin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Regeneration follows a defined sequence including initial injury and inflammatory response (degradation and epidermal closure days 7–10).
source: Regeneration follows a defined sequence, including (i) initial injury and inflammatory response (degradation and epidermal closure days 7–10), (ii) anabolic cell dedifferentiation, recruitment, and proliferation during formation of the critical blastema (day 10), and (iii) differentiation (day 14 and later) in which the bone is regenerated via direct intramembranous ossification (Han et al., 2008; Fernando et al., 2011; Simkin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Regeneration includes anabolic cell dedifferentiation, recruitment, and proliferation during formation of the critical blastema (day 10).
source: Regeneration follows a defined sequence, including (i) initial injury and inflammatory response (degradation and epidermal closure days 7–10), (ii) anabolic cell dedifferentiation, recruitment, and proliferation during formation of the critical blastema (day 10), and (iii) differentiation (day 14 and later) in which the bone is regenerated via direct intramembranous ossification (Han et al., 2008; Fernando et al., 2011; Simkin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Regeneration includes differentiation (day 14 and later) in which the bone is regenerated via direct intramembranous ossification.
source: Regeneration follows a defined sequence, including (i) initial injury and inflammatory response (degradation and epidermal closure days 7–10), (ii) anabolic cell dedifferentiation, recruitment, and proliferation during formation of the critical blastema (day 10), and (iii) differentiation (day 14 and later) in which the bone is regenerated via direct intramembranous ossification (Han et al., 2008; Fernando et al., 2011; Simkin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proliferating skeletal progenitors and differentiated osteoblasts exhibit different levels and types of cell metabolism.
source: As a result, proliferating skeletal progenitors and differentiated osteoblasts exhibit different levels and types of cell metabolism (van Gastel and Carmeliet, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Proliferating progenitors require ATP for energy and carbon for biomass.
source: Proliferating progenitors require ATP for energy and carbon for biomass (Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011) and are highly glycolytic (Salazar-Noratto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proliferating progenitors are highly glycolytic.
source: Proliferating progenitors require ATP for energy and carbon for biomass (Lunt and Vander Heiden, 2011) and are highly glycolytic (Salazar-Noratto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Glycolytic dependency increases in differentiated osteoblasts due to the high metabolic demand of matrix and amino acids synthesis.
source: This glycolytic dependency increases in differentiated osteoblasts due to the high metabolic demand of matrix and amino acids synthesis (van Gastel and Carmeliet, 2021; Capulli et al., 2014; Bonewald, 2011; Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The aging process disrupts cell metabolism by decreasing NAD+ levels.
source: The aging process disrupts cell metabolism by decreasing NAD+ levels (Neri and Borzì, 2020; Song et al., 2019) and mitochondrial function and content (Yu et al., 2018; Bellantuono et al., 2009), leading to a loss of osteogenic potential.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The aging process disrupts cell metabolism by decreasing mitochondrial function and content.
source: The aging process disrupts cell metabolism by decreasing NAD+ levels (Neri and Borzì, 2020; Song et al., 2019) and mitochondrial function and content (Yu et al., 2018; Bellantuono et al., 2009), leading to a loss of osteogenic potential.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Aging-related disruption of cell metabolism leads to a loss of osteogenic potential.
source: The aging process disrupts cell metabolism by decreasing NAD+ levels (Neri and Borzì, 2020; Song et al., 2019) and mitochondrial function and content (Yu et al., 2018; Bellantuono et al., 2009), leading to a loss of osteogenic potential.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and logical inference.

claim: Recent papers have made use of single-cell RNA sequencing to generate a blastema-specific gene signature.
source: To this end, recent papers have made use of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) to generate a blastema-specific gene signature (Storer et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing is unable to provide spatial context to identified transcriptional profiles.
source: While these published works were able to provide incredible insight into the cellular heterogeneity of the blastema, scRNAseq is unable to provide spatial context to these identified transcriptional profiles.
evidence: This is a known limitation of scRNAseq technology.

claim: Identifying the spatial localization of signals that drive limb regeneration is critical for discerning mechanisms that drive limb patterning and timing of differentiation.
source: Identifying the spatial localization of the signals that drive limb regeneration is a critical piece in discerning the mechanisms that drive limb patterning and the timing of differentiation during this multi-tissue process (Bassat and Tanaka, 2021; Storer and Miller, 2020; Johnson and Lehoczky, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Spatial transcriptomics yielded approximately 4500 spatial 'spots' containing approximately 1900 unique genes (nFeature) and approximately 5500 unique transcripts (nCount) per spot.
source: This technique yielded ~4500 spatial 'spots' containing ~1900 unique genes (nFeature) and ~5500 unique transcripts (nCount) per spot (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) at a spatial resolution of 55 µm, corresponding to ~5–10 cells per spatial spot, depending on the relative location within the blastema.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Spatial transcriptomics has a spatial resolution of 55 µm, corresponding to approximately 5–10 cells per spatial spot.
source: This technique yielded ~4500 spatial 'spots' containing ~1900 unique genes (nFeature) and ~5500 unique transcripts (nCount) per spot (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) at a spatial resolution of 55 µm, corresponding to ~5–10 cells per spatial spot, depending on the relative location within the blastema.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the spatial transcriptomics method.

claim: Spatially restricted gene expression was confirmed by using positive marker genes for the epithelium (Krt14) and bone (Bglap2).
source: Spatially restricted gene expression and image registration was confirmed by using positive marker genes for the epithelium (Krt14) and bone (Bglap2), by expression of previously proposed blastema markers Pdgfra (Storer et al., 2020) and Mest (Johnson et al., 2020; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pdgfra is a previously proposed blastema marker.
source: Spatially restricted gene expression and image registration was confirmed by using positive marker genes for the epithelium (Krt14) and bone (Bglap2), by expression of previously proposed blastema markers Pdgfra (Storer et al., 2020) and Mest (Johnson et al., 2020; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mest is a previously proposed blastema marker.
source: Spatially restricted gene expression and image registration was confirmed by using positive marker genes for the epithelium (Krt14) and bone (Bglap2), by expression of previously proposed blastema markers Pdgfra (Storer et al., 2020) and Mest (Johnson et al., 2020; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Hematopoietic cells infiltrate the digit at relatively high numbers after injury.
source: Conversely, although hematopoietic cells infiltrate the digit at relatively high numbers after injury (Simkin et al., 2017), these cells are present in a more diffuse pattern, surrounded by other cell types.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hematopoietic cells are present in a diffuse pattern, surrounded by other cell types, resulting in minimal detection of CD45 (encoded by Ptprc).
source: Conversely, although hematopoietic cells infiltrate the digit at relatively high numbers after injury (Simkin et al., 2017), these cells are present in a more diffuse pattern, surrounded by other cell types. This resulted in minimal detection of the hematopoietic cell marker CD45 (encoded by Ptprc) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and logical inference about spatial resolution limitations.

claim: 829 differentially expressed genes were enriched in the blastema.
source: These results identified 829 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in the blastema, 146 of which were also enriched within the 337 boundary spot DEGs, and no overlap with the 214 DEGs identifying the remaining digit (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 146 genes were enriched in both the blastema and boundary regions.
source: These results identified 829 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in the blastema, 146 of which were also enriched within the 337 boundary spot DEGs, and no overlap with the 214 DEGs identifying the remaining digit (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no overlap between blastema DEGs and the 214 DEGs identifying the remaining digit.
source: These results identified 829 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) enriched in the blastema, 146 of which were also enriched within the 337 boundary spot DEGs, and no overlap with the 214 DEGs identifying the remaining digit (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pathway analysis on blastema DEGs showed enrichment in gene ontology terms linked to cellular bioenergetics.
source: Interestingly, pathway analysis on blastema DEGs showed enrichment in gene ontology terms linked to cellular bioenergetics, in addition to major signaling pathways such as transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ), PI3K-Akt, and MAPK (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Pathway analysis on blastema DEGs showed enrichment in TGFβ, PI3K-Akt, and MAPK signaling pathways.
source: Interestingly, pathway analysis on blastema DEGs showed enrichment in gene ontology terms linked to cellular bioenergetics, in addition to major signaling pathways such as transforming growth factor beta (TGFβ), PI3K-Akt, and MAPK (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The spatially derived blastema signature showed a high degree of specificity for the regenerating blastema and minimal labeling of the remaining digit tissue.
source: Module scoring, reflecting the average expression of a selected gene list relative to random gene list controls, and spatial localization of our blastema signature showed a high degree of specificity for the regenerating blastema and minimal labeling of the remaining digit tissue (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: All blastema signatures showed preferential enrichment within the blastema region relative to other regions of the digit.
source: All blastema signatures showed preferential enrichment, to varying extents, within our blastema region relative to other regions of the digit, further validating this spatial transcriptomics technique (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The spatial transcriptomics-derived blastema gene signature had a high specificity for the blastema in both scRNAseq data sets.
source: Module scoring confirmed the spatial transcriptomics-derived blastema gene signature had a high specificity for the blastema in both scRNAseq data sets, distinguishing the blastema fibroblasts from other cell types, and specifically excluded more mature osteogenic clusters (cluster 6 from Storer et al. data and cluster 5 from Johnson et al. data).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The spatial transcriptomics-derived blastema gene signature specifically excluded more mature osteogenic clusters.
source: Module scoring confirmed the spatial transcriptomics-derived blastema gene signature had a high specificity for the blastema in both scRNAseq data sets, distinguishing the blastema fibroblasts from other cell types, and specifically excluded more mature osteogenic clusters (cluster 6 from Storer et al. data and cluster 5 from Johnson et al. data).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Specific labeling of the blastema could be achieved using a reduced gene list of approximately 5 genes (Edil3, Mmp14, Chrdl1, Ptx3, and Bmp5).
source: These results demonstrate that, although no single gene was able to show efficient labeling of the entire blastema, specific labeling of the blastema could be achieved using a reduced gene list of ~5 genes (Edil3, Mmp14, Chrdl1, Ptx3, and Bmp5).
evidence: This is supported by reductive iteration analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: No single gene was able to show efficient labeling of the entire blastema.
source: These results demonstrate that, although no single gene was able to show efficient labeling of the entire blastema, specific labeling of the blastema could be achieved using a reduced gene list of ~5 genes (Edil3, Mmp14, Chrdl1, Ptx3, and Bmp5).
evidence: This is supported by reductive iteration analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Aged mice showed no difference in the timing of the histolytic event (D7) compared to young mice.
source: These data revealed that, while aged mice showed no difference in the timing of the histolytic event (D7), a marked delay in the transition from blastema to anabolic bone formation was observed.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Aged mice showed a marked delay in the transition from blastema to anabolic bone formation.
source: These data revealed that, while aged mice showed no difference in the timing of the histolytic event (D7), a marked delay in the transition from blastema to anabolic bone formation was observed.
evidence: This is supported by histological and micro-CT data shown in Figure 2.

claim: New bone was observed at D14 in young mice.
source: While new bone was observed at D14 in young mice, new bone wasn't observed in aged mice until D21.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: New bone wasn't observed in aged mice until D21.
source: While new bone was observed at D14 in young mice, new bone wasn't observed in aged mice until D21.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The delay in mineralization in aged mice was associated with a reduction in trabecular bone volume and thickness.
source: This delay in mineralization was associated with a reduction in trabecular bone volume and thickness, and a concordant increase in trabecular spacing (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The delay in mineralization in aged mice was associated with an increase in trabecular spacing.
source: This delay in mineralization was associated with a reduction in trabecular bone volume and thickness, and a concordant increase in trabecular spacing (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Pathway analysis identified enrichment in several pathways linked to cell proliferation in the aged blastema.
source: Pathway analysis of DEGs showing differential expression in the young or old blastema identified several potentially important factors altered in our impaired regeneration model (Figure 3A). First, we identified enrichment in several pathways linked to cell proliferation in the aged blastema.
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant increase in S-phase and G2M-phase scoring in the aged blastema.
source: Using CellCycleScoring frequently employed in scRNAseq analysis (Nestorowa et al., 2016), our data demonstrated a significant increase in S-phase and G2M-phase scoring in the aged blastema (Figure 3B), resulting in a significant redistribution of blastema and boundary spots into a proliferative phase (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle scoring data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a significant redistribution of blastema and boundary spots into a proliferative phase in aged mice.
source: Using CellCycleScoring frequently employed in scRNAseq analysis (Nestorowa et al., 2016), our data demonstrated a significant increase in S-phase and G2M-phase scoring in the aged blastema (Figure 3B), resulting in a significant redistribution of blastema and boundary spots into a proliferative phase (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle distribution data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Increased proliferation in aged blastema was confirmed histologically by staining for the proliferation marker PCNA.
source: This increased proliferation in aged blastema was confirmed histologically by staining for the proliferation marker PCNA (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Aged mice demonstrated a predominant increase in genes linked to both entry into, and progression through, the cell cycle.
source: Blastema from young and old digits were further interrogated for genes linked to cell cycle activity, including genes encoding cyclins, as well as components of the anaphase promoting complex (Figure 3E). These data show a predominant increase in genes linked to both entry into, and progression through, the cell cycle in aged mice, further supporting an increased cell proliferation in the regenerating blastema of aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Aged mice showed notable reductions in the Hippo, WNT, and TGFβ pathways.
source: Whole blastema analysis shows notable reductions in the Hippo, WNT, and TGFβ pathways in aged mice, with SpatialTime analyses suggesting that both Hippo and WNT signaling are preferentially decreased distally in aged mice, while TGFβ signaling was decreased proximally, but had comparable expression distally (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Hippo and WNT signaling are preferentially decreased distally in aged mice.
source: Whole blastema analysis shows notable reductions in the Hippo, WNT, and TGFβ pathways in aged mice, with SpatialTime analyses suggesting that both Hippo and WNT signaling are preferentially decreased distally in aged mice, while TGFβ signaling was decreased proximally, but had comparable expression distally (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by SpatialTime analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TGFβ signaling was decreased proximally in aged mice, but had comparable expression distally.
source: Whole blastema analysis shows notable reductions in the Hippo, WNT, and TGFβ pathways in aged mice, with SpatialTime analyses suggesting that both Hippo and WNT signaling are preferentially decreased distally in aged mice, while TGFβ signaling was decreased proximally, but had comparable expression distally (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by SpatialTime analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Analysis of the aged blastema showed enrichment for DEGs linked to cellular bioenergetics.
source: Beyond morphogenetic pathways, analysis of the aged blastema also showed enrichment for DEGs linked to cellular bioenergetics, and that these metabolic pathways were divergently regulated in young and aged mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Metabolic pathways were divergently regulated in young and aged mice.
source: Beyond morphogenetic pathways, analysis of the aged blastema also showed enrichment for DEGs linked to cellular bioenergetics, and that these metabolic pathways were divergently regulated in young and aged mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Metabolic analysis showed increased glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation in the blastema of aged mice.
source: Metabolic analysis showed increased glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) in the blastema of aged mice, resulting in an increased overall energetic response (cumulative glycolysis and OxPhos scoring) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Aged mice showed an increased overall energetic response (cumulative glycolysis and OxPhos scoring).
source: Metabolic analysis showed increased glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) in the blastema of aged mice, resulting in an increased overall energetic response (cumulative glycolysis and OxPhos scoring) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The increased bioenergetic signature was specific for glucose metabolism, as scoring of fatty acid metabolism failed to show any significant increase.
source: This increased bioenergetic signature was specific for glucose metabolism, as scoring of fatty acid metabolism failed to show any significant increase.
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Aging upregulates the TCA cycle and complexes IV and V of the electron transport chain.
source: A more detailed analysis of respiratory energy metabolism suggests that aging upregulates the TCA cycle and complexes IV and V of the electron transport chain, with no significant change in mitophagy or mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Aging shows no significant change in mitophagy or mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: A more detailed analysis of respiratory energy metabolism suggests that aging upregulates the TCA cycle and complexes IV and V of the electron transport chain, with no significant change in mitophagy or mitochondrial biogenesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glycolysis is preferentially upregulated within the proximal blastema of aged digits.
source: Applying our SpatialTime technique, we observed that glycolysis is preferentially upregulated within the proximal blastema of aged digits and OxPhos increased in the distal blastema (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by SpatialTime analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: OxPhos is increased in the distal blastema of aged digits.
source: Applying our SpatialTime technique, we observed that glycolysis is preferentially upregulated within the proximal blastema of aged digits and OxPhos increased in the distal blastema (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by SpatialTime analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Oxygen consumption rates associated with basal respiration, ATP, maximal respiration, and non-mitochondrial respiration were higher in the aged blastema-derived cells.
source: Oxygen consumption rates (OCR) associated with basal respiration (p<0.05), ATP (p<0.05), maximal respiration (p<0.05), and non-mitochondrial respiration (p<0.05) were higher in the aged blastema-derived cells.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) was significantly higher after each stressor injection in aged blastema-derived cells.
source: The extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) (Mito Stress Test) was also significantly higher after each stressor injection, suggesting increased glycolytic rates.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Glycolytic Rate Assay confirmed a significant increase in the capacity for aged blastema cells to respond to glucose by upregulating compensatory glycolysis.
source: The Glycolytic Rate Assay (Seahorse analysis) confirmed a significant increase in the capacity for aged blastema cells to respond to glucose by upregulating compensatory glycolysis (p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Intracellular hypoxia is an integral component of digit regeneration.
source: We have previously shown that intracellular hypoxia is an integral component of digit regeneration (Sammarco et al., 2014; Simkin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Spatial transcriptomics module scoring and histological labeling using hypoxyprobe both confirm elevated levels of hypoxia within the blastema of aged mice.
source: Spatial transcriptomics module scoring (Figure 5A), as well as confirmatory histological labeling using hypoxyprobe (Figure 5B), both confirm elevated levels of hypoxia within the blastema of aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 5A and hypoxyprobe staining shown in Figure 5B.

claim: VEGF signaling showed significant elevations within the blastema of aged mice.
source: To determine whether this shift in hypoxic signaling was associated with shifts in downstream levels of VEGF signaling, and subsequent vascularization, we quantified each of these parameters in our spatial data using module scoring. Both VEGF signaling (Figure 5C) and vascular markers (Figure 5D) showed significant elevations within the blastema of aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Vascular markers showed significant elevations within the blastema of aged mice.
source: To determine whether this shift in hypoxic signaling was associated with shifts in downstream levels of VEGF signaling, and subsequent vascularization, we quantified each of these parameters in our spatial data using module scoring. Both VEGF signaling (Figure 5C) and vascular markers (Figure 5D) showed significant elevations within the blastema of aged mice.
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Aged mice demonstrated increased gene expression for vessel markers concentrated predominantly in the proximal portion of the blastema.
source: SpatialTime analysis confirmed that aged mice demonstrated increased gene expression for vessel markers concentrated predominantly in the proximal portion of the blastema (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by SpatialTime analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Blastemas from young mice showed minimal expression of vessel markers concentrated mostly in the distal tip.
source: This is in contrast to blastemas from young mice that showed minimal expression of vessel markers concentrated mostly in the distal tip (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by SpatialTime analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Large, CD31+ vessels were predominantly seen in the distal tip of the blastema in young mice.
source: Histological analyses confirmed that while large, CD31+ vessels were predominantly seen in the distal tip of the blastema in young mice, additional small and/or immature vessels were detected throughout the blastemas of aged mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Additional small and/or immature vessels were detected throughout the blastemas of aged mice.
source: Histological analyses confirmed that while large, CD31+ vessels were predominantly seen in the distal tip of the blastema in young mice, additional small and/or immature vessels were detected throughout the blastemas of aged mice (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Increased intracellular hypoxia and altered vessel patterning persisted throughout the healing process in aged mice.
source: Interestingly, this increased in intracellular hypoxia and altered vessel patterning persisted throughout the healing process in aged mice, with significantly greater hypoxyprobe labeling and CD31+ blood vessels present throughout the regenerating digit at D42 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Changes in vascularization were accompanied by altered regenerative bone architecture characterized by multidirectional and disorganized void space in the aged mice.
source: These changes in vascularization were accompanied by altered regenerative bone architecture characterized by multidirectional and disorganized void space in the aged mice and an overall increased inner void fraction (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Aged mice showed an overall increased inner void fraction in regenerated bone.
source: These changes in vascularization were accompanied by altered regenerative bone architecture characterized by multidirectional and disorganized void space in the aged mice and an overall increased inner void fraction (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Lee et al. demonstrated that active glycolysis in the mature osteoblast relies heavily on the malate-aspartate shuttle.
source: Lee et al. recently demonstrated that active glycolysis in the mature osteoblast relies heavily on the malate-aspartate shuttle (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The malate-aspartate shuttle serves to move OAA into the mitochondria by first converting it to malate.
source: This shuttle serves to move OAA into the mitochondria by first converting it to malate. Once inside the mitochondrial membrane malate is oxidized back to OAA again, generating NADH directly in the mitochondria for use in the electron transport chain (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: OAA has been shown to promote brain mitochondrial biogenesis and increase ATP production in nerves via systemic application.
source: To this end we utilized the anapleurotic metabolite OAA, which has been shown to promote brain mitochondrial biogenesis and increase ATP production in nerves via systemic application (Wilkins et al., 2016; Wilkins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Seahorse analysis on aged blastemas revealed a significant decrease in maximal respiration after the addition of OAA.
source: In vitro, Seahorse analysis on aged blastemas using the Mito Stress Test revealed a significant decrease in maximal respiration after the addition of OAA, with no significant change in ECAR or glycolytic flux (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: OAA treatment showed no significant change in ECAR or glycolytic flux in aged blastemas.
source: In vitro, Seahorse analysis on aged blastemas using the Mito Stress Test revealed a significant decrease in maximal respiration after the addition of OAA, with no significant change in ECAR or glycolytic flux (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse analysis data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Significant increases in regenerated bone volume and thickness were observed in response to daily OAA treatment from D10 to D28.
source: 3D micro-CT image analysis of skeletal regeneration after OAA treatment revealed that while only slight increases in regenerative bone parameters were observed by day 21, significant increases in regenerated bone volume and thickness were observed in response to daily OAA treatment from D10 to D28 (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by micro-CT data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The increase in bone after OAA treatment is predominantly within the first 0.4 mm of the bone stump, rather than the distal end of the bone.
source: 2D analysis of the regenerated bone at day 28 post amputation, oriented along the axis of healing from the proximal to distal end, demonstrated that this increase in bone is predominantly within the first 0.4 mm of the bone stump, rather than the distal end of the bone (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by 2D micro-CT analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: OAA further increased the number of cells in S-phase and G2M-phase scoring in both the fibroblast and bone areas of the regenerating digit.
source: Cell cycle analysis revealed that OAA further increased the number of cells in S-phase and G2M-phase scoring in both the fibroblast and bone areas of the regenerating digit (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle scoring data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The increase in proliferation after OAA treatment was confirmed histologically by staining for the proliferation marker PCNA.
source: This increase in proliferation was confirmed histologically by staining for the proliferation marker PCNA (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: OAA treatment increased hypoxia expression levels in the fibroblast area and reduced hypoxia expression levels in bone area of the D21 aged digits.
source: Spatial transcriptomics module scoring (Figure 7D), as well as confirmatory histological labeling using hypoxyprobe (Figure 7E), both showed that OAA treatment increased hypoxia expression levels in the fibroblast area and reduced hypoxia expression levels in bone area of the D21 aged digits.
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 7D and hypoxyprobe staining shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Hypoxia values after OAA treatment were inversely correlated with VEGF signaling.
source: These values were inversely correlated with VEGF signaling, while vascular markers were found to be decreased in both regions (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Vascular markers were found to be decreased in both fibroblast and bone regions after OAA treatment.
source: These values were inversely correlated with VEGF signaling, while vascular markers were found to be decreased in both regions (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: OAA administration resulted in increased glycolysis in both the fibroblast and bone areas.
source: Treatment with OAA was also found to affect cell metabolism, with OAA administration resulting in increased glycolysis in both the fibroblast and bone areas, while OxPhos was found to be increased only within the fibroblast region (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: OxPhos was found to be increased only within the fibroblast region after OAA treatment.
source: Treatment with OAA was also found to affect cell metabolism, with OAA administration resulting in increased glycolysis in both the fibroblast and bone areas, while OxPhos was found to be increased only within the fibroblast region (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: WNT signaling was found to be upregulated in both the fibroblast and bone regions after OAA treatment.
source: To determine the effects of OAA or morphogenetic signaling, we assessed modular scoring of pathway activation (Figure 7H). WNT signaling was found to be upregulated in both the fibroblast and bone regions, while BMP signaling was increased in the fibroblast region and decreased in the bone region.
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: BMP signaling was increased in the fibroblast region and decreased in the bone region after OAA treatment.
source: To determine the effects of OAA or morphogenetic signaling, we assessed modular scoring of pathway activation (Figure 7H). WNT signaling was found to be upregulated in both the fibroblast and bone regions, while BMP signaling was increased in the fibroblast region and decreased in the bone region.
evidence: This is supported by module scoring data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Cell metabolism plays an important role in regulating blastema function and regenerative potential.
source: In this study, we report an important role for cell metabolism in regulating blastema function and regenerative potential.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Impaired digit regeneration in aged mice is associated with increased proliferation and decreased bone building.
source: Our results show impaired digit regeneration in aged mice, associated with increased proliferation and decreased bone building, as well as differential proximal-distal patterning of glycolysis and OxPhos.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: Aged mice show differential proximal-distal patterning of glycolysis and OxPhos.
source: Our results show impaired digit regeneration in aged mice, associated with increased proliferation and decreased bone building, as well as differential proximal-distal patterning of glycolysis and OxPhos.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: Increased metabolic demands in aged mice are associated with increased intracellular hypoxia, VEGF signaling, and vascularization.
source: These increased metabolic demands in aged mice are associated with increased intracellular hypoxia, VEGF signaling, and vascularization.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: Administration of the metabolite OAA can partially rescue age-dependent decline in regeneration.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that administration of the metabolite OAA can partially rescue this age-dependent decline in regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: For highly regenerative animals like the Mexican axolotl, age is associated with a decline in regenerative capacity.
source: Even for highly regenerative animals like the Mexican axolotl (McCusker et al., 2015), age is associated with a decline in regenerative capacity (Seifert and Voss, 2013; Vieira et al., 2020; McCusker and Gardiner, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In humans, while regenerative capacity of the digit tips persists into adulthood, fidelity of regeneration appears to decline with age.
source: Similarly, in humans, while regenerative capacity of the digit tips persists into adulthood, fidelity of regeneration appears to decline with age (Muneoka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Age is associated with a delay in the switch from bone catabolism to bone anabolism.
source: We show here that age is associated with a delay in the switch from bone catabolism to bone anabolism, and that the final regenerate has significantly increased trabecular spaces, reduced volume, and overall impaired bone patterning, suggesting a defect in bone anabolism in aged mice.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: The final regenerate in aged mice has significantly increased trabecular spaces, reduced volume, and overall impaired bone patterning.
source: We show here that age is associated with a delay in the switch from bone catabolism to bone anabolism, and that the final regenerate has significantly increased trabecular spaces, reduced volume, and overall impaired bone patterning, suggesting a defect in bone anabolism in aged mice.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: The delay in bone regeneration is accompanied by increased proliferation, which may indicate delays in cell cycle progression in the aged blastema.
source: This delay is accompanied by increased proliferation, which may indicate that delays in bone regeneration may be linked to delays in cell cycle progression in the aged blastema.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Increased proliferation in the aged blastema may explain the increases in cell metabolism, since proliferation would require both energy and biosynthesis.
source: Increased proliferation in the aged blastema may also explain the increases in cell metabolism, since proliferation would require both energy and biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Most studies agree that formation of the blastema relies on, at least in part, the dedifferentiation of terminal cells within the remaining digit.
source: Most studies agree that formation of the blastema relies on, at least in part, the dedifferentiation of terminal cells within the remaining digit (Storer et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2020; Lehoczky et al., 2011; Rinkevich et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proliferation is thought to play a relatively less critical role in blastema formation.
source: In contrast, proliferation is thought to play a relatively less critical role in blastema formation (Storer et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased proliferation may point to a potential loss of plasticity, and the subsequent loss of dedifferentiation within aged cells.
source: While our studies are not able to determine the relative contribution of dedifferentiation to blastema formation in young and aged mice due to the lack of reliable markers, this increased proliferation may point to a potential loss of plasticity, and the subsequent loss of dedifferentiation within aged cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The increased intracellular hypoxia may be suppressing osteoblast differentiation.
source: Another possible explanation for the delay is that the increased intracellular hypoxia may be suppressing osteoblast differentiation, a concept demonstrated in both osteoblasts (Utting et al., 2006) and in the blastema (Sammarco et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VEGF expression is intimately linked to bone repair and regeneration.
source: VEGF expression is intimately linked to bone repair and regeneration (Hu and Olsen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Intramembranous ossification relies on hypoxia-induced VEGF expression to increase formation of vasculature and mobilize bone progenitors.
source: Intramembranous ossification relies on hypoxia-induced VEGF expression (Wang et al., 2007) to increase formation of vasculature and mobilize bone progenitors (Hu and Olsen, 2016; Matsubara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Excess VEGF is known to inhibit the function of pericytes, leading to formation of immature blood vessels and uncoupling of angiogenesis and osteogenesis.
source: However, excess VEGF is also known to inhibit the function of pericytes (Greenberg et al., 2008), leading to formation of immature blood vessels and uncoupling of angiogenesis and osteogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Excess VEGF signaling has been shown to inhibit digit regeneration in neonates.
source: In addition, excess VEGF signaling has also been shown to inhibit digit regeneration in neonates (Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Excess VEGF production driven by hypoxia in the blastema of aged mice may contribute to altered bone architecture and impede regeneration.
source: Together, these data suggest that excess VEGF production driven by hypoxia in the blastema of aged mice may contribute to altered bone architecture and impede regeneration in aged mice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on experimental results and previous literature.

claim: In vitro studies suggest that hypoxia may be directly driven by oxygen consumption by the electron transfer chain in mitochondria.
source: However, in vitro studies (Kurokawa et al., 2015; Prior et al., 2014) suggest that this hypoxia may be directly driven by oxygen consumption by the electron transfer chain in mitochondria (Friedman and Nunnari, 2014) and continues to be an ongoing area of research (Agathocleous and Harris, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Yao et al. confirmed that intracellular hypoxia modulates epigenetic modifications.
source: A recent study by Yao et al., 2019, confirmed this same phenomenon in bone in vivo, noting that intracellular hypoxia modulates epigenetic modifications (Batie et al., 2019; Chakraborty et al., 2019; Gallipoli and Huntly, 2019), as well as gene and protein expression (Semenza, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Yao et al. demonstrate that the use of non-oxidative glycolysis protects hypoxic tissues from anoxia by regulating intracellular hypoxia during development.
source: Functionally, Yao et al. demonstrate that the use of non-oxidative glycolysis protects hypoxic tissues from anoxia by regulating intracellular hypoxia during development.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lee et al. show that reduced oxygen consumption is a hallmark of osteoblasts.
source: Lee et al. fortify this finding by showing that reduced oxygen consumption is a hallmark of osteoblasts (Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Upregulation of OxPhos during skeletal regeneration in aged mice facilitates hypoxia-driven vasculature that ultimately disrupts bone architecture.
source: Guided by our results, and in concert with these published findings, we propose that upregulation of OxPhos during skeletal regeneration in aged mice facilitates hypoxia-driven vasculature that ultimately disrupts bone architecture.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on experimental results and previous literature.

claim: OAA provides a source of both NADH and biomass.
source: We sought to address the unmet energy needs of the aged blastema with OAA, given that mature osteoblasts rely heavily on the malate-aspartate shuttle (Lee et al., 2020), and that OAA provides a source of both NADH and biomass (Stephanopoulos et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: OAA partially resolved the aged phenotype by increasing bone volume and thickness, but did not decrease trabecular spacing.
source: Phenotypically, OAA partially resolved the aged phenotype by increasing bone volume and thickness, but did not decrease trabecular spacing.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: OAA-dependent changes were accompanied by increases in WNT pathway expression in both fibroblasts and bone.
source: These OAA-dependent changes were accompanied by increases in WNT pathway expression in both fibroblasts and bone, which may be driving these anabolic bone processes.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results with speculative interpretation.

claim: The regulatory axis between WNT and cell metabolism has only recently begun to be explored in bone.
source: The regulatory axis between WNT and cell metabolism has only recently begun to be explored in bone, and while evidence has grown showing the impact of WNT on cell metabolism (Karner and Long, 2017; Karner et al., 2015; Kobayashi et al., 2016), data is scarce in understanding the converse relationship where cell metabolism modulates WNT signaling (Costa et al., 2019; Delgado-Deida et al., 2020; Risha et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: WNT is a central regulator of bone repair and regeneration, and is known to differentially affect various cell lineages.
source: WNT is a central regulator of bone repair and regeneration, and is known to differentially affect various cell lineages (Houschyar et al., 2018), which may partially explain the divergent effects in fibroblasts and bone.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ROS production after tail amputation in Xenopus is necessary for regeneration, possibly through WNT signaling and proliferation.
source: ROS production after tail amputation in Xenopus is necessary for regeneration, possibly through WNT signaling and proliferation (Love et al., 2013), and leptin and melanocortin 4 receptor, key molecules regulating energy balance, are critical in tadpole tail regeneration (Love et al., 2011) and digit regeneration (Kang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Leptin and melanocortin 4 receptor, key molecules regulating energy balance, are critical in tadpole tail regeneration and digit regeneration.
source: ROS production after tail amputation in Xenopus is necessary for regeneration, possibly through WNT signaling and proliferation (Love et al., 2013), and leptin and melanocortin 4 receptor, key molecules regulating energy balance, are critical in tadpole tail regeneration (Love et al., 2011) and digit regeneration (Kang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Increased metabolism levels may be an inherent and essential part of limb regeneration.
source: While we chose OAA partially because it supplemented the elevated cell metabolism levels seen at D10, these increased metabolism levels may be an inherent and essential part of limb regeneration, with OAA potentially providing building blocks for cell growth and expansion, further increasing cell metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Optimal permeabilization is a balance between RNA release and excess diffusion that results in loss of spatial specificity.
source: Optimal permeabilization is a balance between RNA release and excess diffusion that results in loss of spatial specificity.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of the spatial transcriptomics method.

claim: The balance in permeabilization does not promote the complete recovery of mRNA within the overlaid tissue section, restricting the capture efficiency of the transcriptome.
source: This balance does not promote the complete recovery of mRNA within the overlaid tissue section, restricting the capture efficiency of the transcriptome.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of the spatial transcriptomics method.

claim: The level of transcriptional information obtained per spatial spot is consistent with typical drop-seq-based single-cell experiments.
source: Analytically, while our results suggest that the level of transcriptional information obtained per spatial spot is consistent with typical drop-seq-based single-cell experiments, the latter relies on a large sample size to help computationally 'fill in' dropout transcriptional information with that of its co-clustering neighbors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Spatial information likely reflects a similar loss of transcriptional information but without the availability of thousands of spots to compensate.
source: Our spatial information likely reflects a similar loss of transcriptional information but without the availability of thousands of spots to compensate.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the spatial transcriptomics method.

claim: Each spatial spot represents the transcriptome from multiple cells, making it unable to distinguish cell heterogeneity within close proximity.
source: Another limitation is the low resolution, with each spatial spot representing the transcriptome from multiple cells. As such, we are unable to distinguish cell heterogeneity within close proximity.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of the spatial transcriptomics method.

claim: The lack of Ptprc expression likely reflects the fact that immune cells are scattered among other cell types, resulting in 'masking' of their individual transcriptome.
source: This lack of Ptprc expression likely reflects the fact that immune cells are scattered among other cell types, resulting in 'masking' of their individual transcriptome.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the spatial transcriptomics method.

claim: Time course studies suggest regeneration delays occur at the level of osteogenic commitment and mineralization.
source: This study addresses a direct comparison of young and aged digit regeneration where our data support an age-dependent delay in bone regeneration. To address differences in gene expression, we analyze both the aged and young blastema 10 days after amputation. While time course studies suggest regeneration delays occur at the level of osteogenic commitment and mineralization, using day 10 for both ages may capture differences that are merely representative of a chronological shift.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Studies in hypoxia and proliferation suggest that gene expression differences are not simply a delay.
source: Our studies in hypoxia and proliferation suggest that these gene expression differences are not simply a delay, however it is important to take this possibility into consideration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: Pro-osteogenic transcriptional changes observed at D21, prior to any significant changes in bone architecture, suggests that OAA-mediated rescue functions upstream of the mineralization process to promote cell fate determination.
source: While pro-osteogenic transcriptional changes observed at D21, prior to any significant changes in bone architecture, suggests that OAA-mediated rescue, at least in part, functions upstream of the mineralization process to promote cell fate determination, we cannot rule out the possibility that OAA may act at the level of promoting osteoblast mineralization during bone formation and late-stage remodeling.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Spatial transcriptomics provides spatial registration of blastema gene expression differences in aged and young mice.
source: This study provides spatial registration of blastema gene expression differences in aged and young mice, and confirms prior expression profiles of the blastema (Storer et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contributions.

claim: Cell metabolism is altered during aging, resulting in impaired regeneration.
source: Our data suggest that cell metabolism is altered during aging, resulting in impaired regeneration, and that while administration of the metabolite OAA is able to enhance bone formation, it is only able to partially rescue the phenotype.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Administration of the metabolite OAA is able to enhance bone formation, but is only able to partially rescue the phenotype.
source: Our data suggest that cell metabolism is altered during aging, resulting in impaired regeneration, and that while administration of the metabolite OAA is able to enhance bone formation, it is only able to partially rescue the phenotype.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: OAA-dependent regeneration is driven, at least in part, by upregulation of canonical WNT signaling.
source: Furthermore, our data show that OAA-dependent regeneration is driven, at least in part, by upregulation of canonical WNT signaling.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results.
